PHP Group Discloses New Unpatched Remote Code Execution Flaw Following PHP2Shell Updates

The PHP Group disclosed a new unpatched remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-115560) affecting session handlers, following emergency patches for two critical PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619).

**If you run PHP, first make sure you’ve applied the emergency PHP2Shell patches from two days ago, then turn off session upload progress (session.upload_progress.enabled = Off) unless you actually need it, which blocks this new flaw. posts.content:
----------------

🛠️ Tool
===================

php2shell-scanner: high-fidelity exposure detection for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

Searchlight Cyber's research team (the group formerly known as Assetnote) released an open-source scanner for the php2shell vulnerability pair. The team has been through this cycle before, both with wp2shell, which it discovered itself, and with react2shell late last year. Each of these high-impact web-stack issues raises the same detection problem: maximize coverage while minimizing false positives and false negatives. This release is their answer for the current one.

Why another scanner

Scanners published in the wake of the disclosure mostly rely on version checks, or fail to represent the vulnerable conditions accurately for both mod_php and php-fpm. Version-only signals fail in two directions: flagging hosts that are actually patched, or missing hosts where the banner does not reflect exploitable conditions. The logic was first implemented inside the Searchlight Exposure platform, and the standalone version is now public.

How the check works

Detection is progressive, in three tiers:

1. Controlled OOM trigger. The scanner attempts to produce a PHP memory-exhaustion error. The vulnerability fundamentally requires an out-of-memory condition, so there is no reliable way to confirm exploitability without inducing it.
2. Differential empty HTTP 500. Next, it observes responses for a differential empty HTTP 500, which the authors describe as a PHP-FPM worker failure.
3. Version fallback. Only when behavioral checks do not settle the question does it fall back to whether the target advertises a known unpatched PHP version.

Risk profile

The authors are direct about this: triggering an OOM condition is inherently risky, and that is the price of reliable detection here. In the majority of PHP installations a worker crash recovers quickly and should not cause disruption, but the writeup explicitly asks for care and caution when scanning. Practical translation: don't fire this at capacity-constrained production systems during peak traffic.

Context around the disclosure

Initial information on the vulnerability was incomplete, followed quickly by a wave of auto-generated, low-quality PoCs that added noise rather than clarity. Searchlight credits Calif's writeup with settling most of the open questions. The detection logic served Searchlight Exposure customers first, then was released publicly so anyone can determine exposure with the same rigor.

Practical notes
• Exposure validation across mixed PHP estates where mod_php and php-fpm behave differently
• Prioritization: behavioral tiers are stronger evidence than version matches
• Scheduling: run behavioral checks away from peak load, and treat the version fallback tier as weaker evidence by design
• The tool is newly released and not personally tested; this summary reflects the vendor writeup, not an independent accuracy assessment

References
• Repository: assetnote/php2shell-scanner on GitHub
• Authors: Shubham Shah, Adam Kues, Patrik Grobshäuser, Kevin Gervot
• Related: Calif's writeup on php2shell

posts.content:
----------------

🛠️ Tool
===================

php2shell-scanner: high-fidelity exposure detection for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

Searchlight Cyber's research team (the group formerly known as Assetnote) released an open-source scanner for the php2shell vulnerability pair. The team has been through this cycle before, both with wp2shell, which it discovered itself, and with react2shell late last year. Each of these high-impact web-stack issues raises the same detection problem: maximize coverage while minimizing false positives and false negatives. This release is their answer for the current one.

Why another scanner

Scanners published in the wake of the disclosure mostly rely on version checks, or fail to represent the vulnerable conditions accurately for both mod_php and php-fpm. Version-only signals fail in two directions: flagging hosts that are actually patched, or missing hosts where the banner does not reflect exploitable conditions. The logic was first implemented inside the Searchlight Exposure platform, and the standalone version is now public.

How the check works

Detection is progressive, in three tiers:

1. Controlled OOM trigger. The scanner attempts to produce a PHP memory-exhaustion error. The vulnerability fundamentally requires an out-of-memory condition, so there is no reliable way to confirm exploitability without inducing it.
2. Differential empty HTTP 500. Next, it observes responses for a differential empty HTTP 500, which the authors describe as a PHP-FPM worker failure.
3. Version fallback. Only when behavioral checks do not settle the question does it fall back to whether the target advertises a known unpatched PHP version.

Risk profile

The authors are direct about this: triggering an OOM condition is inherently risky, and that is the price of reliable detection here. In the majority of PHP installations a worker crash recovers quickly and should not cause disruption, but the writeup explicitly asks for care and caution when scanning. Practical translation: don't fire this at capacity-constrained production systems during peak traffic.

Context around the disclosure

Initial information on the vulnerability was incomplete, followed quickly by a wave of auto-generated, low-quality PoCs that added noise rather than clarity. Searchlight credits Calif's writeup with settling most of the open questions. The detection logic served Searchlight Exposure customers first, then was released publicly so anyone can determine exposure with the same rigor.

Practical notes
• Exposure validation across mixed PHP estates where mod_php and php-fpm behave differently
• Prioritization: behavioral tiers are stronger evidence than version matches
• Scheduling: run behavioral checks away from peak load, and treat the version fallback tier as weaker evidence by design
• The tool is newly released and not personally tested; this summary reflects the vendor writeup, not an independent accuracy assessment

References
• Repository: assetnote/php2shell-scanner on GitHub
• Authors: Shubham Shah, Adam Kues, Patrik Grobshäuser, Kevin Gervot
• Related: Calif's writeup on php2shell

posts.content:
🚨 This time the bug isn’t in your code, it’s in PHP itself.

PHP2Shell is two CVEs in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) that can lead to unauthenticated RCE.

When something like this lands, the first question is usually: what exactly is affected, and what do I need to patch?

I’d rather answer that from the terminal than from twelve browser tabs.

With the ZEN SecDB CLI:

1️⃣ secdb search php2shell

finds both CVEs.

2️⃣ secdb cve CVE-2026-109618

gives the full record: description, CVSS 4.0 at 9.2, CVSS 3.1 at 9.8, vectors, references and vendor advisories from Debian, Red Hat, SUSE, Ubuntu, Arch, Gentoo, FreeBSD and others.

That’s useful because you can quickly check whether your distro already ships a fix, instead of going through each security tracker manually.

If you run PHP, upgrade to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or use the patched package provided by your distro.

Configuration mitigations may reduce the risk, but they don’t replace patching.

And if the server was exposed, it’s probably worth checking whether it was already compromised.

posts.content: Ptain n'importe quoi le mec il bosse chez haproxy et il avait même pas patché la CVE CVE-2026-90678

CVE-2026-90678.description: An issue was discovered in HAProxy 3.3.0 through 3.4.4 and in 3.5-dev1 through 3.5-dev5. Exploitation requires an HTTP/3 frontend: HAProxy must be built with QUIC support and configured with a QUIC bind listener, and the affected traffic must reach a backend over HTTP/1.1 using chunked transfer coding on a reused connection. Under those conditions, when an HTTP/3 request carries no Content-Length header, the HTTP/3 multiplexer credits the length declared in a DATA frame header to the stream endpoint's known-input-payload estimate at the moment the frame header is decoded, before the payload has been received, and that declared length is emitted verbatim as the HTTP/1.1 chunk size. A remote unauthenticated client that declares more payload than it delivers and then ends the stream causes HAProxy to announce a chunk larger than the bytes it writes and to return the connection to the idle pool in a desynchronized state. The result is potential HTTP request smuggling on reused backend connections: an attacker can place a request past a frontend rule such as a path-based http-request deny, so that the smuggled request is never seen by HAProxy's HTTP analysis, and can cause concurrent clients' requests, including their request lines and Authorization headers, to be consumed as the attacker's request body and lost. Exploitation is not deterministic; it depends on a race with backend connection pooling, succeeding in a majority of but not all trials during testing, and can be retried freely. The mechanism was introduced in 3.3-dev10; releases 3.2.x and earlier are unaffected.

CVE-2026-79979.description:
The arm64 MMU backend invalidates a single virtual address from the TLB with invalidate_tlb_page() in arch/arm64/core/mmu.c, which issued TLBI VAE1{IS} with an operand of virt >> 12. That operand encodes the ASID in bits [63:48], so the invalidation only ever matched ASID 0 (the kernel page tables) and global entries. Memory domains, however, are allocated ASIDs starting at 1 in arch_mem_domain_init(), and every domain-private leaf created by private_map() is mapped with MT_NG, i.e. non-global. A domain's cached translation therefore survived the invalidation.

All callers of invalidate_tlb_page() are demand-paging paths. When the eviction algorithm reclaims a frame, page_frame_prepare_locked() in kernel/mmu.c calls arch_mem_page_out(), which marks the kernel leaf invalid, propagates the invalid descriptor into every domain via sync_domains(), and then flushes only ASID 0. do_page_fault() immediately reuses the very same page frame for the incoming mapping through arch_mem_page_in(). A user thread that had already touched the evicted page — a k_mem_partition added with arch_mem_domain_partition_add(), or its own stack mapped by map_thread_stack() — retains a valid EL0 read/write translation to that physical frame under its own ASID.

Unprivileged code running in a user thread can drive memory pressure to force eviction and then keep accessing the stale address, obtaining read and write access to whatever the kernel subsequently placed in that frame: supervisor data, another memory domain's partition, or another thread's stack. This defeats the isolation that CONFIG_USERSPACE is meant to enforce, allowing information disclosure and memory corruption up to full compromise of the system.

The fix switches the implementation to TLBI VAAE1{IS}, which matches every ASID and both global and non-global entries, so no domain-tagged translation survives a page out, dirty-bit update or access-flag clear. Exploitation requires an arm64 build with both CONFIG_USERSPACE and CONFIG_DEMAND_PAGING enabled, an active backing store, and at least one demand-paged page that is also privately mapped into a user memory domain. The same commit additionally stops globalize_table() from stripping EL0 permission and non-global attributes off domain-private leaves during paging synchronization, which previously caused user threads to lose access to their own partitions and stacks.

CVE-2026-79977.description:
The WireGuard VPN service in subsys/net/lib/wireguard/wg.c updated the peer endpoint from a message it could not authenticate. In handle_transport_data(), when the 32-bit receiver index of an incoming transport-data message matched no session, the code both scheduled a new handshake and copied the datagram's source address into peer->endpoint with memcpy(&peer->endpoint, peer_addr, sizeof(peer->endpoint)). Because the receiver index is unknown, there is no key with which such a message could be verified, so the address written into peer->endpoint is entirely attacker-supplied. Every other endpoint update in the implementation happens only after authentication — after the Noise handshake in handle_handshake_init(), or after AEAD decryption plus the anti-replay check in wg_process_data_message().

The WireGuard listener is registered with net_udp_register() using no remote address or port filter and defaults to UDP port 51820 (CONFIG_WIREGUARD_PORT), and wg_ctrl_recv() resolves the peer by interface rather than by any cryptographic identity. Any host able to send a UDP datagram to that port can therefore reach the defect off-path, with no need to observe legitimate traffic: a 16-byte datagram carrying the transport-data type, zeroed reserved bytes and an arbitrary receiver index is sufficient. The vulnerable branch runs whenever the peer has neither a valid handshake nor a current keypair — the state at boot and after a session expires.

A single spoofed datagram redirects peer->endpoint to an address of the attacker's choosing, and all subsequent handshake initiations, keepalives and encrypted data packets are sent there. The legitimate peer never receives the initiations and so never re-authenticates, and nothing resets the endpoint afterwards, leaving the tunnel persistently unusable on devices whose peer does not initiate handshakes itself. The attacker can also relay the redirected initiations to the real peer to place itself in the path of the tunnel, observing ciphertext and traffic metadata and selectively dropping packets. WireGuard's end-to-end cryptography still prevents decryption or forgery of tunnel content, so the impact is loss of availability plus limited confidentiality, not key compromise.

The fix removes the endpoint learning from this path entirely: the stale-session recovery is kept, but the handshake is sent only to an endpoint learnt from an authenticated message, falling back to the configured cfg_endpoint, and the message is dropped when neither is known. CONFIG_WIREGUARD is marked experimental and is not enabled by default.

CVE-2026-79982.description:
The Bluetooth HCI USB transport class of the new USB device stack, subsys/usb/device_next/class/bt_hci.c, copies every controller-to-host HCI packet into a USB transfer buffer before enqueuing it on an endpoint. bt_hci_tx_sync_in() allocated that buffer from bt_hci_ep_pool, a fixed pool whose slots are only USBD_MAX_BULK_MPS bytes (64 on full-speed-only builds), and then performed net_buf_add_mem(buf, bt_buf->data, bt_buf->len) with no length check. HCI event and ACL buffers are sized by CONFIG_BT_BUF_EVT_RX_SIZE and CONFIG_BT_BUF_ACL_RX_SIZE and can be far larger, so the copy runs past the end of the 64-byte slot into the adjacent slots and into whatever follows the statically allocated pool.

The device runs the local Bluetooth controller in raw HCI mode (CONFIG_BT_HCI_RAW), so the oversized packets originate over the air. With the HCI buffer sizes recommended for full-featured controllers, an unauthenticated attacker within Bluetooth range can supply the overflowing bytes: a connected peer that negotiates Data Length Extension can send ACL fragments up to CONFIG_BT_CTLR_DATA_LENGTH_MAX bytes, and an attacker that merely broadcasts extended advertising data reaches the same path through LE Extended Advertising Report events, which the controller fragments only to CONFIG_BT_BUF_EVT_RX_SIZE. In the stock configuration the overflow is already reached without any radio traffic: the mandatory Read Supported Commands command-complete event is 70 bytes and overruns the 64-byte slot by six bytes on every host initialization.

Because net_buf_add_mem() validates tailroom only through an assertion unless CONFIG_NET_BUF_HARDENING is enabled, builds with CONFIG_ASSERT=n — the usual production setting — silently corrupt memory adjacent to the USB buffer pool with attacker-chosen contents, which on a target without memory protection between subsystems can lead to arbitrary code execution. Builds with assertions enabled fail the assertion instead and panic, giving a remotely triggerable denial of service. The fix introduces a separate bt_hci_tx_pool sized to MAX(BT_BUF_ACL_RX_SIZE, BT_BUF_EVT_RX_SIZE) for the controller-to-host direction while leaving the host-to-device pool at the endpoint packet size, which is already bounds-checked during reassembly.

CVE-2026-115419.description:
**Summary**  
Strands Agents SDK is an open-source SDK, available for Python (strands-agents) and TypeScript (@strands-agents/sdk), for building and running AI agents. An issue exists where, under certain circumstances, the Agent2Agent (A2A) server shares conversation history across callers with different context\_id values, allowing one caller to read and influence another caller's session.  
  
**Impact**  
The A2A server did not properly isolate conversation state between callers. In multi-tenant deployments, an authenticated remote user could access another caller's conversation history or influence model behavior for other callers (CWE-488: Unintended Disclosure of Data Element to Wrong Session). This affects any deployment where an A2A server is reachable by more than one user or tenant.  
  
**Impacted versions:**  
strands-agents (Python): all versions containing the multiagent.a2a module, < 1.43.0  
@strands-agents/sdk (TypeScript): < 1.5.0  
  
**Patches**  
This issue has been addressed in strands-agents version 1.43.0 and @strands-agents/sdk version 1.5.0. The A2A server now uses an agent factory so conversation state is isolated per A2A context\_id. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.  
  
**Workarounds**  
There is no workaround that fully addresses this issue in affected versions. Until you upgrade, do not expose an A2A server to more than one user or tenant. If multiple callers need access, run a separate A2A server instance for each user or tenant.  
  
**References**  
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, we ask that you contact AWS Security via our [vulnerability reporting page](https://aws.amazon.com/security/vulnerability-reporting) or directly via email to [aws-security@amazon.com](mailto:aws-security@amazon.com). posts.content:
"Signal has resolved a critical-severity vulnerability that could allow a malicious caller to keep audio and video tracks enabled even after the user hung up.

The security defect is tracked as CVE-2026-113380 (CVSS score of 9.3) and impacts RingRTC, the open source library Signal uses for voice and video calls, which is based on WebRTC.

Due to the issue, a remote peer could flood the call’s Finite State Machine (FSM) event queue with junk, and the call would not terminate.

This happened because the hangup was not treated as a kill switch, but as an event added to the FSM event queue; there was no rate limit on peer-originated events; and the hangup event had no priority.

“Flood the queue with junk and the hang-up waits behind attacker noise forever, so the call (microphone, possibly camera) is never torn down,” a GitHub write-up by a researcher reads.

By exploiting the vulnerability, an attacker could keep the audio and video tracks flowing from a target device while the victim believes they ended the call.

The security defect was resolved in RingRTC version 2.72.0, which was released on September 4.

Details on the flaw, however, were published on Tuesday, along with a conceptual proof-of-concept (PoC). NIST added the CVE to the NVD database on Tuesday.

Signal resolved the issue by ensuring that call termination requests do not remain blocked in FSM’s event queue and are detected independently.

Users should update their Signal applications as soon as possible. Otherwise, they should check the call indicator to make sure the call indeed ended."
https://www.securityweek.com/signal-vulnerability-lets-malicious-callers-block-hang-ups/

CVE-2026-107685.description:
Improper Certificate Validation vulnerability in the WebSocket streaming client in agentjido req_llm allows an on-path attacker to read and modify OpenAI WebSocket sessions, including the authorization bearer token, via a TLS certificate the client does not trust. ReqLLM.Streaming.WebSocketSession.Client.start/3 in lib/req_llm/streaming/web_socket_session/client.ex starts WebSockex without TLS options, and WebSockex defaults to insecure: true, which connects with verify: :verify_none. The option allowlist also drops any caller-supplied cacerts or ssl_options, so an application cannot turn verification on.

The OpenAI Responses, Realtime, and Codex WebSocket paths reach this client and send the API key or OAuth access token in the authorization header. HTTP streaming through Finch and the HTTP/2 duplex session through Mint verify certificates and are not affected.

This issue affects req_llm: from 1.9.0 before 1.29.0.

posts.content: CVE-2026-54630 (CRITICAL): Part-DB-server <2.12.1 lets authenticated users upload .phar files, enabling remote code execution as www-data. Patch to 2.12.1+ and restrict user permissions. https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-54630-cwe-434-unrestricted-upload-of-file-with-dangerous-type-in-part-db-part-db-server-3e3f77096f8d900f #OffSeq #CVE #RCE #infosec

CVE-2026-54630.description: Part-DB is an open source inventory management system for electronic components. Prior to version 2.12.1, the part attachment upload handler stores uploaded files under the web-served media directory using the client-supplied file extension, and its extension blocklist does not include phar. AttachmentSubmitHandler::renameBlacklistedExtensions() rewrites dangerous extensions (php, phtml, sh, cgi, py, js, html, htaccess, ...) to .txt, but phar is absent from the list, so a .phar file keeps its extension. Public attachments (the default) are written into public/media/, which is the Apache document root. The shipped Apache configuration routes .phar to PHP-FPM, so the stored file is executed as PHP on request. The per-attachment-type extension filter is empty by default and is not consulted by the upload handler in a way that blocks this, and a non-admin user in the default users group can create an attachment type with no filter and attach files to parts. Any authenticated user in the default users group uploads a .phar attachment to a part and fetches it under /media/, executing arbitrary PHP as the www-data web user. Ability to exploit depends on the webserver config, docker image contained the vulnerability by default. This issue has been patched in version 2.12.1.
